item.title: Cyber watch, week of 16 to 22 November 2026: Optimizely, vCenter, Java4Shell, Iran
item.description:
Bulletin for the week of 16 to 22 November, published on 23 November 2026.

Optimizely compromised: 178 major websites served malicious code.

Key points

  1. A script provider, Optimizely, was compromised on 16 November: 178 major websites, including Air France and Ledger, served for a day code that stole bank cards and cryptocurrency.
  2. Two major flaws to fix: VMware vCenter, secretly exploited since September by a China-linked group, and Java4Shell, which affects Java in many enterprise software products.
  3. France officially accused Iran of sabotaging supermarket fridges, and the National Assembly adopted the Résilience bill that transposes NIS2.
  4. The CNIL reminds everyone of the basics with a EUR 5 million fine for passwords stored in clear text.

This week’s topics

Optimizely compromised: malicious code injected into the sites of 178 organisations, including Air France

Supply chain · Critical

item.title: Cyber watch, week of 9 to 15 November 2026: Maileva, N-able, Outlook, NIS2
item.description:
Bulletin for the week of 9 to 15 November, published on 16 November 2026.

Key points

  1. The biggest leak of the week comes from a subcontractor: Maileva (La Poste) announces the theft of data on 22 million mail recipients.
  2. On the vulnerability side, N-able N-central is being compromised even on up-to-date servers, Barracuda confirms intrusions, and Microsoft patches an Outlook flaw that is already being exploited.
  3. In France, the National Assembly rewrote the NIS2 transposition law (final vote on 17 November) and the CNIL fined ten local authorities over their cybersecurity.
  4. The SGS vehicle inspection networks confirm their incident: beware of fake fine text messages.

This week’s topics

Maileva (La Poste): data on 22 million people stolen

Data leak · Critical

item.title: Sabotaged fridges: the second wave hits Europe and blood supplies
item.description:
Weekly bulletin, week of 2 to 8 November 2026.

The essentials

  1. The campaign against connected fridges is spreading: six European countries and plasma freezers of the EFS (the French blood establishment) were targeted on the night of 1 to 2 November, and US agencies issued an alert.
  2. On the vulnerability side, OpenSSH (“sshole”), WordPress and Zyxel switches are being exploited: updates are the priority.
  3. In France, a giant leak is claimed at SGS (vehicle inspection), and the RN confirms its own.
  4. Binance reveals that North Korean attackers got in as early as June via employee workstations, while Chainalysis admits it exposed the access credentials of all its customers.

Sabotaged fridges: second wave in Europe, EFS hit, US alert

Industrial attack · Critical · Follow-up

item.title: Binance: $6.3 billion stolen by North Korea
item.description:
Weekly bulletin, week of 27 October to 1 November 2026.

The essentials

  1. The largest cryptocurrency theft in history: $6.3 billion stolen from Binance, attributed by the FBI to the North Korean group TraderTraitor.
  2. October’s vulnerabilities turn into real attacks: PHP2Shell compromises Palo Alto firewalls, and GitLab, Brotli and a new Cisco flaw are confirmed as exploited.
  3. In France, the wave of leaks hitting political parties continues (PRG, Écologistes, RN) and a second teenager is indicted over the tax-authority hack.
  4. Belgium shuts down its tax authority’s online services after a cyberattack, and the CNIL (the French data protection authority) fines Fnac €7 million for trackers set without consent.

Binance: $6.3 billion stolen, the biggest theft in history

Attack · Critical

item.title: Actil: health data of 61,000 hearing-aid policyholders leaked
item.description:
Daily bulletin of 27 October 2026.

The essentials

  1. In France, a file attributed to Actil, which handles third-party payment (tiers payant) for hearing aids, allegedly exposes the health data and social security numbers of about 61,000 policyholders, mostly elderly; the leak is not confirmed.
  2. In Japan, GMO refuses a $50 million ransom after up to 26,739 virtual desktops were hacked, while in Europe fake “IT support” calls on Teams open the door to ransomware.
  3. PHP2Shell enters CISA’s KEV catalog, but Unit 42 withdraws the European intrusion case it had attributed to it.

Actil: a file on 61,000 hearing-aid policyholders released for free

Data leak · Important

item.title: PHP2Shell: the first real intrusions are confirmed
item.description:
The essentials

  1. Five days after the fixes, PHP2Shell moves from attempts to successful intrusions: a honeypot confirms code execution and a European administration has been compromised.
  2. In France, the hacker ChimeraZ adds 905,097 rows of licence plate data to their claims, while Renaissance and LFI deny any intrusion.
  3. On the defence side, two reports show that stealing a token (Microsoft 365, GitHub) is often worth more to attackers than a password.

PHP2Shell: first successful intrusion confirmed, a European administration hit

Vulnerability · Critical · Follow-up

item.title: Claimed leaks at LFI, Renaissance and the PCF by the same hacker
item.description:
The essentials

  1. A hacker, ChimeraZ, claims campaign-data leaks at three French political parties (LFI, Renaissance, PCF); the figures are unverified.
  2. On the vulnerability side, a Collabora Online flaw is being exploited to booby-trap Nextcloud servers, and a Brotli compression flaw forces Node.js, Python and others to patch one by one.
  3. HPE fixes eight critical flaws in Aruba Wi-Fi, and Kaspersky shows that an up-to-date PC can remain vulnerable if Secure Boot revocations are not enabled.

The same hacker claims leaks at LFI, Renaissance and the PCF

Data breach · Important

item.title: Data breach at the PCF: nearly 190,000 people exposed
item.description:
The essentials

  1. In France, the Communist Party (PCF) confirms the leak of its members’ and supporters’ file, and the French Sailing Federation announces more than 2 million records exposed.
  2. On the network equipment side, Fortinet is pushing urgent patches without detailing the flaws, and an Arista VeloCloud zero-day is being exploited; one hacker has already stolen more than 70,000 credentials from VPNs and firewalls.
  3. In Europe, the Russian group APT28 spied on a shipyard and a NATO military engine maker.

Leaks in France: the PCF, the Sailing Federation and ENGIE affected

Data breach · Important

item.title: PHP2Shell: exploitation began four days before the alert
item.description:
The essentials

  1. PHP2Shell: Amazon saw a first attack as early as 17 October, before the fixes were published. Millions of attempts followed, but no successful takeover is confirmed at this stage.
  2. Trusted tools remain targeted: a Chinese group used AI agents to attack via ConnectWise, and the AI library LiteLLM was published booby-trapped for about two hours.
  3. In France, the French Shooting Federation confirms its leak and Ircantec data is being put up for sale. In Africa, Interpol announces 1,462 arrests.

PHP2Shell: attacks had begun before the fixes

Vulnerability · Critical · Follow-up

item.title: Launch edition: the last ten days in seven stories
item.description:
First bulletin: it catches up on the major stories since 12 October. Future bulletins will only cover news from the last 24 hours and real developments in stories already being followed.

The essentials

  1. Two critical flaws in PHP have been massively attacked since 21 October: public websites were taken offline in France and across Europe.
  2. Attacks increasingly target the physical world (supermarket refrigeration) and trusted tools (booby-trapped updates).
  3. Ransomware: unpatched VPNs and firewalls remain the number one way in.

PHP2Shell: two critical PHP flaws force websites offline across Europe

Vulnerability · Critical

item.title: Why ransomware remains a major threat
item.description:
Context

Ransomware attacks keep rising and hit large companies as well as small businesses, hospitals and local authorities.

Despite better awareness, this type of attack remains one of the most profitable for cybercriminals.

What is happening

Attackers mainly exploit:

  • unpatched vulnerabilities
  • services exposed on the Internet
  • human error (phishing, weak passwords)

Once access is gained, data encryption is often preceded by data theft, which increases the pressure on victims.

Why it matters

Ransomware is no longer only a technical problem:
